builder_plan.scenario: A narrow, repeated product task may not need your largest model.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a released student model fits the task before generating training data.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current model and an off-the-shelf small model on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Student quality, serving cost, teacher calls, training cost, and failures on unusual inputs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
summary: The method replaces token-level statistical watermark detectors by querying a suspect model through its API, mapping generated text to gradient representations with a fixed clean probe model, projecting out ordinary fine-tuning directions, and testing residual alignment with a key-specific watermark basin. It costs maintaining a fixed clean probe model, extra API queries to the suspect model, and embedding the watermark during teacher output generation, but it does not require access to the suspect model's weights or logits. It can fail when the watermark was not embedded in teacher traces, when the key or basin is mismatched, when detection is run at stricter n-gram settings where true-positive rates drop, or when the probe model or task-direction estimate poorly matches the deployment setting.
rationale: This is production-relevant for API providers concerned about distillation abuse, but it should be validated on the reader's own teacher, watermarking pipeline, and suspect-model traffic before operational adoption.

claims.statement: The method replaces token-level statistical watermark detectors by querying a suspect model through its API, mapping generated text to gradient representations with a fixed clean probe model, projecting out ordinary fine-tuning directions, and testing residual alignment with a key-specific watermark basin. It costs maintaining a fixed clean probe model, extra API queries to the suspect model, and embedding the watermark during teacher output generation, but it does not require access to the suspect model's weights or logits. It can fail when the watermark was not embedded in teacher traces, when the key or basin is mismatched, when detection is run at stricter n-gram settings where true-positive rates drop, or when the probe model or task-direction estimate poorly matches the deployment setting.

At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively).
